newsitem.title: HONDURAS: Two dead as rioting escalates in Honduran jails.
newsitem.headline: Two dead as rioting escalates in Honduran jails.

text.p: Two prisoners were shot to death in a riot at a Honduran jail, the latest in a series of riots this week due to massive overcrowding in the country's prisons, authorities said on Thursday.

With 205 fugitives still at large following a mass jailbreak on Monday, Honduran politicians clamored for a crackdown and the nation's military chief said he was prepared to send the army in to any of the nation's 24 prisons to impose order.
A penitentiary in the western city of Santa Rosa de Copan was the third in three days to be torched by inmates late on Wednesday, and police said guards shot two rioters dead in the revolt.
"The jail is just rubble. Two prisoners died in the riot and two more were injured," Wendy Arita, police spokeswoman in Santa Rosa de Copan, some 170 miles (270 km) west of Tegucigalpa, told Reuters.
The 420 prisoners in Santa Rosa de Copan on Thursday continued a protest that has so far spread to four prisons over insanitary conditions and massive overcrowding. They are demanding pardons.
The riots began on Monday when inmates in a jail in Santa Barbara, 110 miles (180 kms) northwest of Tegucigalpa, burned it to the ground and 482 fled in the confusion.
Police said on Thursday that 277 had been recaptured, but the remaining 205 were at large, and a police and army dragnet was proving complicated to enforce.

"It's a slow and difficult task because we're talking about an extensive, mountainous area. But we'll continue the operation until we get them all," said Col. Anael Perez, an official involved in the chase.
The Honduran prison system has a total of 9,650 inmates, 4,650 more than the jails were intended to house. Less than 10 percent of the prisoners have been formally sentenced.

"It's a time bomb," admitted prison system director Romelia de Artica. She said the government was considering demands for a widespread pardon, or more bail for prisoners, because the country had too little money to build new jails.
